<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but B's rebuttal sequence did more damage that A never fully cleared. B's R1 exposed a real tension in A's captivity/regressivity framing; A partially resolved it by distinguishing flexible vs. captive drivers on the same road, but B then supplied a concrete fix to A's strongest pressure point (the exemption-cliff problem) with the flat per-capita rebate, which A's "dodge" reply weakened but did not fully refute. Crucially, B's B4.5 point — that dedicated bus lanes leave every general lane clogged because nothing prices the marginal trip — went essentially unanswered in A's final speeches, and A's answer to B's Q2 (what threshold of opposition would satisfy CON) stayed vague ("a test of alternatives"), letting B's closing charge of "veto with a review date" land largely unrebutted. A's sequencing argument (London/Stockholm already had transit to build on) was a genuine and underexploited strength that could have been pressed harder in closing, but A's closing mostly recapped rather than closing the loop on B's live chicken-and-egg funding argument. B's opening was clipped for length, a real execution cost, but B recovered the lost framing in later rounds and finished with the sharper, more resolved comparison.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's R1 move exposing the captivity/regressivity tension, followed by A's partial resolution and B's unanswered B4.5 point that bus lanes alone don't solve general congestion, was the most consequential exchange — it left a live, undefended gap in A's case going into closing.</best_rebuttal>
